title: What Is a Vacpack? Definition, Prices & Rules (2026)
metaTitle: What Is a Vacpack? Definition, Prices & Rules (2026) | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A vacpack is a deeply discounted 2-5 night resort stay sold below cost in exchange for attending a timeshare preview. Here is what it costs and how it works.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A vacpack (vacation package) is a deeply discounted short resort stay, usually 2-5 nights, sold below its normal cost because you agree to attend a timeshare or resort "preview" presentation. Across our tracked inventory these run roughly $49-$1,899, with a median of $199.
heroImageAlt: What is a vacpack — a $49-$1,899 discounted stay median $199 with a preview requirement
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A vacpack is a short, deeply discounted resort stay sold below cost in exchange for your time at a timeshare or resort "preview" presentation. Across the 617 deals we track, prices run about $49-$1,899, the median is $199, and 47% openly disclose a required presentation averaging 116 minutes.

"Vacpack" is shorthand for a vacation package, and in this corner of the travel market it means something specific: a subsidized short stay that a resort or broker sells at a loss to get you in the door. The math only works for the seller because a slice of attendees buy a timeshare, so the cheap room is really the price of an audience.

What is a vacpack, exactly?

A vacpack is a discounted 2-5 night resort stay priced far below the retail rate in exchange for you attending a sales presentation. The room is genuine and the discount is real, but the deal is structured around your attendance, not around normal occupancy. That is the single fact that separates a vacpack from an ordinary hotel booking, and it is why the same room can cost a quarter of its published rate.

How does a vacpack actually work?

You pay a flat, usually non-refundable fee up front. In return you get lodging and sometimes extras like a resort credit or show tickets, and you commit to a preview tour of typically 90-120 minutes. Most programs also screen you first with a qualification call, checking age, income, and marital status, because the resort only wants attendees who could plausibly buy. If you don't qualify, the cheap price often disappears.

Vacpack featureTypical reality
Price range$49-$1,899; median $199 across tracked deals
Length2-5 nights
CatchPreview presentation, ~90-120 min (avg disclosed 116)
Who qualifiesUsually 25+, ~$50K+ income, couples attend together

Vacpack characteristics summarized from 617 tracked deals. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does a vacpack matter to a deal shopper?

Because the price is honest but the framing usually isn't. A listing may quote a $915 "retail value" next to a $249 price to make the discount look enormous, when the real question is simply whether $249 for those nights plus a two-hour tour is worth it to you. Our data shows the cheapest live vacpack at $48.86 for Williamsburg and 168 deals under $100, so the floor is genuinely low. The value is in ignoring the inflated rack rate and judging the out-of-pocket cost against what you would otherwise pay.

Common misconceptions about vacpacks

The biggest myth is that a vacpack obligates you to buy something. It does not. You commit only to attending the presentation you booked, and you can walk out with your discounted stay having bought nothing. A second myth is that the low price signals a scam. In reality the price is subsidized on purpose, because the resort profits from the small share of attendees who do buy. A third misconception is that the advertised "retail value" reflects what the trip is worth. It rarely does; it is an anchor. When you strip these myths away, a vacpack is simply a transparent trade of your attention for a cheap room. The people who get burned are usually those who did not read the requirements, missed the qualification criteria, or caved to in-room pressure. Go in knowing the rules and the trade works in your favor, not the seller's.

Key fact: A vacpack is not a scam by definition. It is a legitimate trade: a subsidized room for your attention. The risk is the high-pressure pitch, not the room, so the skill is going in knowing you can decline and walk out with your discounted stay intact.

Some brands run these constantly. Westgate, for example, accounts for 159 of the deals we track, averaging $201 with a $49 floor and about $71 per night, which is why it shows up so often when people search for a cheap Orlando or Gatlinburg trip. If you want to see live examples, browse current vacation deals and sort by price to understand the range before you ever pick up the phone.

Bottom line: a vacpack is one of the cheapest ways to sleep at a resort, as long as you treat the presentation as the cost of admission and go in immune to the sales script. Know the price you are paying, ignore the fantasy retail number, and the trade can be a good one.

title: Timeshare Preview Package: Meaning & How It Works
metaTitle: Timeshare Preview Package: Meaning & How It Works | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A timeshare preview package is a discounted resort stay sold in exchange for attending a sales tour. Here is what it includes, what it costs, and the catch.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A timeshare preview package is a discounted resort stay a developer sells to prospective buyers in exchange for attending a sales presentation, or "preview." It is the industry's formal name for what many travelers call a vacpack, and in our data 47% of such deals openly disclose the required tour.
heroImageAlt: Timeshare preview package meaning — discounted stay for a 90-120 minute sales tour
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A timeshare preview package is a discounted stay a resort developer sells to potential buyers in exchange for attending a sales presentation. It is the same concept as a vacpack, just named the way the industry names it. In our tracked inventory 47% of these deals disclose the tour requirement, which averages 116 minutes.

When a developer wants qualified buyers in front of a salesperson, it packages a cheap stay and calls it a preview. The word "preview" is doing real work: it frames the trip as a chance to sample the resort lifestyle, while the developer's actual goal is a sales tour with you as the audience.

What is a timeshare preview package?

A timeshare preview package is a subsidized short resort stay offered to prospective buyers on the condition that they attend a sales presentation. The lodging is real and the discount is genuine, but access is gated behind the tour and behind a screening process that confirms you fit the developer's buyer profile. Strip away the marketing and it is a trade: a cheap room for a captive audience.

How does a preview package work step by step?

You book and pay a flat fee, pass a qualification call that checks age, income, and marital status, and receive lodging plus sometimes extras. During your stay you attend the presentation, typically 90-120 minutes, where a salesperson pitches ownership. You are free to decline and keep the stay. Some resorts also offer a tour waiver that lets you pay a fee to skip the presentation entirely.

ElementWhat to expect
ScreeningQualification call before the price is honored
Tour lengthCommonly 90-120 min; avg disclosed 116 min
ObligationAttend, not buy
ExtrasResort credit, tickets, meals may be included

Preview-package structure summarized from tracked deals. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does the preview framing matter to a shopper?

Because "preview" softens what is a hard sales environment. Some newer travel-club offers, like Branson's resort-preview packages, market themselves without ever saying "timeshare," yet function the same way. The consumer skill is identical: judge the deal on the price you pay and your ability to decline. Our tracked Westgate previews average $201 with a $49 floor, and 168 of our deals sit under $100, so the discounts are real when you ignore the inflated rack rate printed beside them.

How to evaluate a preview package before booking

Start with the all-in price, not the discount. Ask what you actually pay out of pocket, what the presentation length is in writing, and whether both partners must attend. Next, confirm the qualification criteria so the price does not evaporate on the screening call. Then weigh the extras honestly: a resort credit or show tickets only add value if you would have spent that money anyway and can use them under their restrictions. Finally, decide your walk-away position before you arrive, because the presentation is engineered to move you off it. A preview package is a good deal when the room, dates, and price would tempt you even without the marketing, and the tour is merely the admission fee. If the base offer only looks attractive because of an inflated retail comparison, treat that as a warning sign and compare it against ordinary bookings first.

Key fact: "Preview," "tour," "owner update," and "resort visit" all describe the same thing: a scheduled sales presentation. Recognizing the vocabulary is how you avoid being surprised by the pitch.

Preview packages are the engine behind most of the cheap resort stays you will see advertised. If you understand that the room is subsidized by the sales pitch, you can shop them confidently. Compare current vacation deals to see what real preview prices look like, and go in planning to say no unless the ownership math genuinely works for you.

Treated that way, a preview package is one of the best-value short stays available. The room is legitimate, the discount is measurable, and the only real cost beyond the fee is the time you spend politely declining a sales pitch you were warned about in advance.

title: What Is an "Owner Update"? (It's a Sales Pitch)
metaTitle: What Is an Owner Update? (It's a Sales Pitch) | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: An owner update is a timeshare sales presentation for existing owners, framed as an account review. Here is what it really is and how to handle the pitch.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: An "owner update" is a sales presentation aimed at people who already own a timeshare, framed as a friendly account or benefits review. Despite the name, its purpose is to sell you more points, an upgrade, or an add-on, not to service your account.
heroImageAlt: What is an owner update — a timeshare upsell pitch disguised as an account review
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: An owner update is a timeshare sales presentation aimed at existing owners, marketed as a benefits or account review. Its real goal is to upsell you more points, an upgrade, or a new product, not to update your records. Treat it exactly as you would a first-time preview presentation.

If you already own a timeshare, you have probably been invited to an "owner update," often sweetened with free tickets, a resort credit, or a discounted stay. The name is deliberately reassuring. What actually happens in the room is a sales pitch built around your existing account.

What is an owner update?

An owner update is a sales presentation for current timeshare owners disguised as an account or benefits review. Staff frame it as a chance to "make sure you're using your ownership fully" or to learn about "new options," but the meeting is structured to end in an upgrade offer. The update is the hook; the upsell is the point.

Why is it framed as an update instead of a sale?

Because you are more likely to say yes to a review than to a pitch. As an existing owner, you have already shown you buy, your maintenance-fee and usage history is on file, and a salesperson can tailor the offer to gaps in your account. Framing it as helpful maintenance lowers your guard, which is precisely why the softer name is used. The same psychology powers the inflated retail comparisons used elsewhere in this industry.

What they sayWhat it usually means
"Quick benefits review"Scheduled sales presentation
"New options for owners"Upgrade or additional points for sale
"Just 60-90 minutes"Can run longer if you engage
"Free gift for attending"Incentive to get you in the room

Common owner-update framing. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

How should a deal shopper handle an owner update?

Decide before you walk in that you are not buying today. The gift is yours for attending, not for purchasing, so accept it and keep your answer firm. If anything is presented as a limited-time price that vanishes when you leave the room, treat that urgency as a red flag rather than a reason. A genuinely good upgrade will still be available after you research it independently.

What to do when you're invited to an owner update

Treat the invitation as a scheduling decision, not a loyalty test. If the free gift or discounted stay is worth your time, accept it, but set a firm end time and tell the representative up front that you are not purchasing today. Bring a copy of your current ownership details so you can fact-check any claim made about your account, and write down every figure the salesperson quotes. Be especially wary of "today only" upgrade pricing; a legitimate improvement to your ownership will still exist next week after you have researched it independently. If the meeting runs past the promised length or turns high-pressure, you are free to leave. The gift is compensation for attending, and attending never obligates you to spend a dollar. Handled this way, an owner update becomes a low-cost way to collect a perk while keeping full control of your money and your account.

Key fact: "Owner update," "preview," and "owner benefits review" are all names for a sales presentation. If a free gift is attached and a salesperson will be present, assume you are being sold to.

None of this means owning is a mistake or that every upgrade is bad. It means the update is a sales channel, and you should evaluate any offer with the same skepticism you would bring to a first-time pitch. If you are weighing whether to keep chasing owner perks or simply book cheap stays outright, compare current vacation deals and read our qualification call explainer to see how the same funnel targets new buyers. Go in informed, take the gift, and leave the checkbook at home.

faqs.answer: Only after independent research, never under in-room time pressure. A worthwhile upgrade will still exist after you leave, so refuse any offer framed as vanishing the moment you walk out.

title: Rescission Period: Definition + What to Know (2026)
metaTitle: Rescission Period: Definition + What to Know (2026) | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A rescission period is a legally required window to cancel a timeshare purchase for a full refund. Lengths vary by state and are commonly cited as 3-15 days.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A rescission period is a legally mandated window during which you can cancel a timeshare purchase and receive a refund, no reason required. The length is set by state law and is commonly cited in the 3-15 day range, but the exact count and start date depend on the controlling statute, which you must verify.
heroImageAlt: Rescission period definition — a state-set cancel window commonly cited as 3-15 days
content:
This is not legal advice. VacationDeals.to is a vacation-deal comparison site, not a law firm. Laws change and have exceptions. Verify against the official statute linked on this page and consult a licensed attorney in your state before acting.
Bottom Line Up Front: A rescission period is a legally required window to cancel a timeshare purchase and get your money back, with no reason needed. Its length is set by the state where you signed and is commonly cited somewhere between 3 and 15 days, but the exact number and when the clock starts are governed by that state's statute. Confirm the current text before relying on any deadline.

The rescission period is the single most important consumer protection in a timeshare purchase, because it lets a buyer undo the deal after the high-pressure room is behind them. It exists precisely because these sales happen fast and emotionally, and lawmakers built in a cooling-off window.

What is a rescission period?

A rescission period is a statutory window during which a timeshare buyer can cancel the contract and receive a refund without penalty or explanation. It is a right created by state law, not a courtesy the developer grants, and in most states the developer cannot shorten or waive it by contract. The catch is that it is time-limited and the clock can start at signing or at document delivery, depending on the statute.

How long is the rescission period?

The length is set by the state where the contract was signed and is commonly cited in the range of roughly 3 to 15 days, but this varies and should never be assumed. Many states are frequently described as offering somewhere around 5 to 10 days. Because these counts differ by jurisdiction and can change, treat any specific number as something to verify against the current statute rather than as a fact you can rely on from a summary. When in doubt, act as if you have less time, not more.

QuestionGeneral answer (verify locally)
Who sets the length?The state where you signed the contract
Typical range citedCommonly 3-15 days; confirm exact statute
When does it start?Often signing or document delivery, per statute
Can it be waived?Usually no, but confirm the controlling law

General framework only; the controlling statute governs. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does the rescission period matter to a buyer?

Because it is your only guaranteed exit. Once the window closes, the automatic no-questions right generally disappears and getting out becomes far harder and often expensive. If you signed and have second thoughts, the practical move is to find and read the exact statute for the state on your contract immediately, follow its written-notice requirements precisely, and send cancellation by a traceable method well inside whatever window you believe applies.

Key fact: The rescission right lives in the statute, not in what a salesperson says at the table. If someone tells you there is no cancellation option, that is a reason to read the law yourself, not to give up.

You can avoid the whole question by never signing under pressure in the first place. Our tracked data shows short discounted stays from about $49-$1,899 with a median of $199, so you can enjoy a resort vacpack without ever buying ownership. Browse current vacation deals and read our preview package explainer so you understand what you are and are not committing to before you sit down. The safest position of all is the one where you never need a rescission window, because you attended a presentation for a cheap stay and simply declined the pitch, rather than signing a contract you must then race a statutory clock to unwind.

Reminder — not legal advice: this page is information only. Rescission lengths and rules vary by state and change over time. Verify the controlling statute with its official source and consult a licensed attorney in your state before acting.

title: Timeshare Maintenance Fee: What It Covers & Why It Rises
metaTitle: Timeshare Maintenance Fee: What It Covers & Why It Rises | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A timeshare maintenance fee is an annual charge owners pay for upkeep, staffing, and reserves. Here is what it covers, why it rises yearly, and how to judge it.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A timeshare maintenance fee is a recurring annual charge every owner pays to cover the resort's upkeep, staffing, insurance, and reserve funds. It is mandatory, rises most years, and is the true long-term cost of ownership, separate from whatever you paid to buy in.
heroImageAlt: Timeshare maintenance fee — the mandatory annual cost that rises most years
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A maintenance fee is the mandatory annual charge every timeshare owner pays for the resort's upkeep, staffing, insurance, and reserve funds. It rises most years, it does not stop when the mortgage is paid off, and it is the number that determines whether ownership is a good deal over time.

People shopping timeshares fixate on the purchase price, but the maintenance fee is the cost that actually matters over a lifetime of ownership. It is charged every single year you hold the interest, whether or not you travel, and it tends to climb faster than general inflation.

What is a timeshare maintenance fee?

A timeshare maintenance fee is a recurring annual charge that funds the operation of the resort: cleaning, repairs, landscaping, staff wages, property insurance, utilities, and reserve funds for major renovations. Every owner pays it in proportion to their interest, and it is not optional. Falling behind can trigger penalties, loss of usage rights, and eventually collection or foreclosure action.

Why does the maintenance fee keep rising?

Fees rise because the underlying costs rise: labor, insurance, energy, and building materials all increase over time, and aging resorts need ever-larger reserves for renovations. Owners also cover the share of any owners who default, so as a resort ages and delinquencies grow, the burden on paying owners can accelerate. This is why a fee that looked modest at purchase can feel very different a decade later, long after any purchase discount has faded.

Fee coversWhy it grows
Staffing and wagesLabor costs rise over time
Insurance and utilitiesPremiums and energy prices climb
Reserve fundsAging buildings need bigger renovations
Owner defaultsPaying owners absorb others' unpaid shares

General maintenance-fee drivers. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does the fee matter to a deal shopper?

Because it reframes the whole value question. A cheap purchase price plus a rising annual fee can easily cost more over ten years than simply booking discounted stays as you go. Our tracked inventory shows a median short-stay vacpack price of $199 and 168 deals under $100, with no annual obligation attached at all. For many travelers, paying per trip beats paying a permanent fee that only goes up.

How to project the true cost of maintenance fees

Before buying, ask for three numbers in writing: the current annual maintenance fee, its increase history over the last five to ten years, and any special assessments levied recently. Special assessments are one-off charges on top of the regular fee, often for major repairs or storm damage, and they can be substantial. Use the increase history to project the fee forward across the years you expect to own, then add it to the amortized purchase price. Divide that lifetime total by the nights you realistically expect to use, and you have a true per-night cost you can compare against real market prices. If the salesperson resists providing the increase history or waves off special assessments as rare, treat that as a signal to slow down. The fee is the part of ownership that compounds silently, so the more precisely you model it, the less likely you are to be surprised a decade from now.

Key fact: The maintenance fee never ends. Paying off a timeshare loan does not end the annual fee, and the fee typically rises every year for as long as you own, which is a core reason resale prices are often near zero.

If a salesperson downplays the maintenance fee or refuses to project it forward, treat that as a signal. Ask for the current fee, its increase history, and any special assessments, then compare the lifetime total against booking vacation deals a la carte. Understanding this fee is also central to reading our points-based timeshare explainer, since points ownership carries the same recurring cost. Judge ownership on the fee you will pay forever, not the price you pay once.

title: Deeded vs Right-to-Use Timeshares: The Difference
metaTitle: Deeded vs Right-to-Use Timeshares: The Difference | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Deeded timeshares give you real property ownership; right-to-use gives a contract to use a resort for set years. Here is how the two differ and why it matters.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A deeded timeshare gives you an actual ownership interest in real property that you can hold, will, or sell. A right-to-use timeshare gives you only a contractual right to use a resort for a fixed number of years, after which the right expires and you own nothing.
heroImageAlt: Deeded vs right-to-use timeshare — real property ownership versus a time-limited use contract
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: Deeded timeshares are real property you own indefinitely and can pass on or sell; right-to-use timeshares are a contract to use a resort for a set term that eventually expires. The distinction affects inheritance, resale, and how long your maintenance-fee obligation lasts.

Two people can both "own a timeshare" and hold completely different things. One holds a recorded deed to real estate; the other holds a contract that runs out. Knowing which one is on the table changes what you are actually buying and how you eventually get out.

What is the difference between deeded and right-to-use timeshares?

A deeded timeshare is an ownership interest in real property, recorded like other real estate, that you generally hold indefinitely and can sell, gift, or leave to heirs; a right-to-use timeshare is a contractual license to use a resort for a defined number of years, after which the right simply ends. Deeded is closer to owning; right-to-use is closer to a long prepaid lease.

Why does the deeded-versus-right-to-use distinction matter?

It matters for permanence and exit. A deeded interest can be perpetual, which sounds appealing but also means the maintenance fee obligation can pass to your heirs unless the interest is disposed of. A right-to-use interest ends on a fixed date, capping the obligation, but you own no asset at the end and typically cannot sell it as easily. This permanence question is also the heart of the perpetuity clause legend that circulates on timeshare forums.

DurationOften indefinite / perpetualFixed term, then expires
Inherit / sellGenerally yesLimited; ends at term
Fee obligationCan pass to heirsEnds with the term

General structural comparison; individual contracts vary. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Which is better for a buyer?

Neither is universally better; it depends on what you fear more. If you want an asset you can pass down and potentially resell, deeded fits, but understand the fee can outlive you. If you want a hard stop on the obligation, right-to-use caps it, but you build no equity and exit options are narrower. In practice, resale values for both are often near zero, which is why many travelers skip ownership entirely.

How to tell which type you're being offered

Read the contract, not the brochure. A deeded interest will reference a recorded deed, a real property interest, and language about ownership that can be conveyed or inherited. A right-to-use interest will reference a term of years, a use license, or a membership that ends on a stated date. If the paperwork is vague, ask directly, in writing, whether you are receiving a deeded property interest or a contractual right that expires, and when. The distinction changes your exit options, your estate planning, and how long the maintenance-fee obligation lasts, so it is not a detail to gloss over. Also confirm what happens at the end: a right-to-use interest simply expires and returns nothing, while a deeded interest continues until you actively dispose of it. Neither is inherently better, but signing without knowing which one you hold means you cannot judge the real length of the commitment you are taking on.

Key fact: "Perpetual" ownership is a double-edged word. A deeded, perpetual interest never expires, which means the annual maintenance fee never expires either, unless you successfully transfer or dispose of the interest.

For most people chasing a cheap trip, the cleaner path is to book a discounted stay with no ownership strings. Our tracked inventory shows short vacpacks with a median of $199 and 168 under $100, none of which leave you holding a deed or a decades-long contract. Compare live vacation deals before you let a presentation frame permanent ownership as your only option. And whichever structure you are offered, get the answer in writing, because the difference between owning real property forever and holding a contract that quietly expires is far too consequential to take on a salesperson's verbal summary.

title: Float Week: Meaning, Booking Windows, Gotchas
metaTitle: Float Week: Meaning, Booking Windows, Gotchas | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A float week is a timeshare week you book within a season rather than a fixed date. Here is how float weeks work, their booking windows, and the common gotchas.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A float week is a timeshare week you reserve within an assigned season rather than owning one fixed calendar week. It offers flexibility on paper, but availability is first-come and prime dates get claimed fast, so the flexibility is real only if you book early.
heroImageAlt: Float week meaning — a season-based timeshare week booked first-come, not a fixed date
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A float week lets you book any available week within an assigned season instead of owning a single fixed date. The flexibility is genuine but conditional: reservations are first-come, prime weeks disappear quickly, and booking windows open months ahead, so procrastinators effectively lose the benefit.

Timeshare weeks come in two flavors: fixed and floating. A fixed week is the same calendar week every year. A float week trades that certainty for flexibility, but the flexibility comes with strings that salespeople rarely emphasize.

What is a float week?

A float week is a timeshare week you reserve within a defined season, such as summer or a peak range, rather than a specific fixed date you own outright. You still own a week's worth of usage, but which week you get depends on booking it before other owners in your season claim the same dates. In effect, you own a season and compete for the calendar.

How do float week booking windows work?

Most float programs open reservations a set number of months before the travel date and fill on a first-come basis. That means the most desirable weeks, holidays, school breaks, festival dates, are gone almost immediately when the window opens. To actually use a prime float week, you typically must book at the earliest possible moment, which requires planning far ahead. Miss the opening and you are left with the leftover dates within your season.

Why does a float week matter to a shopper?

Because "flexible" is the selling word, and the gotchas are the fine print. A float week can be great for someone with an open schedule who books the instant windows open, and frustrating for anyone who travels on fixed dates like school holidays that every other owner also wants. Understand the booking window and the season boundaries before you value the flexibility, because a float week you can never book when you need it is worth little.

How to make a float week actually work for you

The single most important habit is knowing your booking window and reserving the instant it opens. Mark the date the window opens for the travel period you want, and be ready to book the moment reservations go live, because prime weeks in your season are claimed within hours. Have backup dates and even backup resorts chosen in advance, so you are not scrambling if your first choice is gone. If your travel is locked to school holidays or specific events that every other owner also wants, be realistic: a float week may frustrate you every year, and a fixed week or paying per trip could serve you better. Also confirm the exact boundaries of your assigned season, since a week that falls just outside it may not be bookable at all. Float ownership rewards planners and punishes procrastinators, so the flexibility is real only if you treat booking day as a fixed appointment.

Key fact: A float week is only as flexible as its calendar. If prime dates in your season book out the day the window opens, your "flexibility" is really an early-booking race you must win every year.

If your travel dates are inflexible, this is worth weighing against simply booking a discounted stay when you need it. Our tracked vacpacks let you pick specific dates and pay per trip, with a median price of $199. Float weeks also interact with points-based systems and exchange companies, so read those before assuming a float week guarantees the trip you want. Compare live vacation deals to see what date-specific booking looks like without ownership.

title: Points-Based Timeshares Explained (With Real Math)
metaTitle: Points-Based Timeshares Explained (With Real Math) | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A points-based timeshare gives an annual allotment of points to book stays across a network instead of one fixed week. Here is how the points math really works.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A points-based timeshare gives you an annual allotment of points you spend to book stays across a resort network, with prices in points varying by resort, unit size, season, and day of week. It replaces a fixed week with a flexible currency, but that currency inflates and its value is set by the developer.
heroImageAlt: Points-based timeshare explained — an annual points currency priced by season and demand
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A points-based timeshare gives you an annual bucket of points to spend booking stays across a network, with each stay costing a different number of points by resort, room size, season, and even day of week. It is flexible, but the developer controls the points charts, so a stay that cost X points this year can cost more later.

Older timeshares sold a fixed week. Modern programs mostly sell points, a flexible internal currency. Points can genuinely be more useful than a rigid week, but they also hide the cost behind a chart only the developer controls, which is exactly why understanding the math matters.

What is a points-based timeshare?

A points-based timeshare gives you a set number of points each year that you redeem to book accommodation within the brand's network, where every stay is priced in points that vary by resort, unit size, season, and day of week. Instead of owning one week, you own spending power. A weekend in peak season at a flagship resort might cost several times what a midweek off-season stay at a smaller property costs.

How does the points math actually work?

Say you own 100,000 points a year. A peak-season week at a top resort might be charged at 80,000 points, while an off-peak midweek stay elsewhere might be 20,000. So your allotment could stretch to several modest trips or one premium week. The catch is that the point charts are not fixed by contract in the way a deeded week is: developers can re-price stays over time, effectively diluting what your points buy, even as your annual maintenance fee keeps rising.

Shoulder week~45,000About two weeks

Illustrative point costs only; each program sets its own charts. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why do points matter to a deal shopper?

Because points make the true cost hard to see. A salesperson can show you a chart where your points unlock a dream vacation, without dwelling on rising fees, chart re-pricing, or the difficulty of ever selling the ownership. To judge a points deal, divide your all-in annual cost, purchase amortized plus maintenance fee, by the nights you realistically book, then compare that per-night figure against real market prices. Our tracked inventory averages about $94 per night and a $199 median across short vacpacks, a useful benchmark.

The questions to ask before buying points

Ask for the current point charts in writing and whether the developer reserves the right to change them, because a chart that can be re-priced can quietly erode your buying power year over year. Ask how many points a stay you actually want, in the season and unit size you would use, costs today, then compare that to your annual allotment to see how many real trips your points buy. Confirm whether unused points roll over, expire, or can be banked, and what that costs. Finally, add the annual maintenance fee to the amortized purchase price and divide by realistic nights to get a true per-night figure. Points programs reward disciplined travelers who book early and use every point, and they punish those who let points lapse or book last-minute. If you cannot see yourself using the full allotment every single year, the flexible currency will quietly cost you more than paying for stays as you go.

Key fact: You do not fully control what your points are worth. Developers can adjust point charts, so points can quietly inflate, meaning the same trip costs more points over time while your fee rises too.

Points suit disciplined travelers who book early and use every point every year. For everyone else, paying per trip avoids the inflation risk entirely. Compare live vacation deals and read our float week explainer, since points and float systems share the same early-booking pressure, before you accept that points ownership beats booking as you go.

title: Rack Rate: The Fake Price Everything Discounts From
metaTitle: Rack Rate: The Fake Price Everything Discounts From | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A rack rate is a resort's highest published price, used as the inflated "before" number that discounts are measured against. Here is why almost nobody pays it.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A rack rate is a hotel or resort's highest published, undiscounted price, the official "before" number. Almost nobody pays it; it exists mainly to make discounts look larger, which is why a $915 rack rate can sit next to a $249 price you actually pay.
heroImageAlt: Rack rate definition — the inflated $915 list price beside the real $249 you pay
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A rack rate is a resort's highest published price, the full sticker figure almost no one actually pays. In vacation-deal marketing it functions as the inflated "before" number that makes a discount look dramatic, which is why you will see a $915 rack rate printed right next to a $249 price you can actually book.

Every big discount needs a big "before" number to be measured against, and in travel that number is the rack rate. Understanding it is the fastest way to stop being impressed by fake savings and start judging deals on what you actually pay.

What is a rack rate?

A rack rate is the highest, official published price a resort lists for a room, before any discount, package, or negotiation. It is the retail sticker of the hotel world, and in practice it is a reference point rather than a price real travelers pay. Corporate rates, package rates, and online prices almost always fall below it, so the rack rate mostly serves as the anchor a discount is calculated from.

Why is the rack rate almost never what you pay?

Because it is designed to be discounted from. Marketers use a high rack rate as a psychological anchor: a $249 deal feels like a steal beside a $915 rack rate, even if $249 is roughly the real market value of those nights. The larger the gap between the rack rate and the offer, the bigger the perceived bargain, which is exactly why the rack rate is quoted so prominently in vacpack listings and resort credit promotions.

Why does the rack rate matter to a deal shopper?

Because it is the number you should ignore. The only figures that matter are the real price you pay and what comparable nights genuinely cost elsewhere. When you strip out the rack-rate theater, our tracked inventory shows a median short-stay price of $199, an average per night around $94, and 168 deals under $100. Judge any offer against those real benchmarks, not against a made-up "before" price.

How to shop past the rack-rate anchor

Build one simple habit: physically ignore the crossed-out number and ask whether the price you actually pay is fair for these nights, in this location, at this time of year. The rack rate is engineered to make you feel a discount rather than evaluate a price, so refusing to react to it is most of the battle. To pressure-test any offer, check what comparable nights cost through ordinary channels, then judge the deal on that gap, not on the advertised savings. Two listings with identical real prices can advertise completely different "savings" simply by inflating the rack rate they discount from, which is proof the savings figure tells you nothing useful. When you consistently benchmark against real market prices instead of the anchor, inflated retail comparisons stop working on you, and you start buying on genuine value. That single discipline defends you against most of the pricing theater in this entire category.

Key fact: A giant "you save $666" claim tells you about the rack rate, not the value. Two offers with identical real prices can advertise wildly different savings simply by inflating the rack rate they discount from.

The habit to build is simple: cover the crossed-out number and ask whether the price you actually pay is fair for the trip. Then compare against live vacation deals and read our vacpack explainer to see typical real prices. Once you stop reacting to rack rates, the fake urgency and inflated savings lose their power and you buy on value alone. That mindset also inoculates you against the countdown timers, "limited rooms left" banners, and other pressure cues that so often accompany an inflated rack rate, because none of them change the one number that matters, the real price you actually pay.

title: Resort Credit: What It Actually Buys (And What It Won't)
metaTitle: Resort Credit: What It Actually Buys (And What It Won't) | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A resort credit is a spending allowance for on-site extras, often restricted to certain vendors and expiring fast. Here is what it really covers and its limits.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A resort credit is a spending allowance the resort gives you for on-site extras like dining, spa, or activities. It is usually restricted to specific vendors, often can't be split across purchases, frequently expires quickly, and rarely converts to cash, so its advertised dollar value overstates what you'll actually use.
heroImageAlt: Resort credit meaning — a restricted on-site allowance worth less than its face value
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A resort credit is a spending allowance for on-site extras, dining, spa, activities, that comes bundled with many vacation deals. It sounds like free money, but restrictions on where, when, and how you can spend it usually mean its real value is far below the dollar figure advertised.

Resort credits are one of the most common sweeteners attached to vacation packages, and one of the most overvalued. The headline number looks generous; the terms quietly ensure you will use only part of it.

What is a resort credit?

A resort credit is an on-property spending allowance you receive as part of a package, redeemable for extras like meals, spa treatments, or activities at the resort. It is not cash and it is not a room discount; it is store credit for the resort's own offerings, which means its value depends entirely on whether you would have spent that money there anyway.

What won't a resort credit do?

It usually won't behave like money. Common restrictions include limiting the credit to specific vendors or outlets, barring it from taxes and gratuities, requiring you to spend it in a single transaction, blocking it on the cheapest items, and expiring it at checkout or even daily. It also rarely converts to cash if unused. These rules are why a "$200 resort credit" can translate to well under $200 of value you actually capture, similar to how a rack rate overstates savings.

Common restrictionEffect on real value

Typical resort-credit restrictions. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does a resort credit matter to a deal shopper?

Because it inflates the perceived value of a package without adding much real value. When you compare two deals, the one advertising a big resort credit is not automatically better; you have to discount the credit by how much of it you will realistically use under its rules. A modest credit you will fully spend beats a large credit hemmed in by restrictions. Treat the credit as a maybe, and judge the deal mostly on the actual price, where our tracked median is $199 and 168 deals sit under $100.

How to value a resort credit before you book

Run every credit through three questions. First, where can it be spent, and are those outlets ones you would actually use? A spa-only credit is worthless to someone who will not book a spa. Second, when does it expire, daily, at checkout, or over the stay, because a credit that resets each day is far smaller than its headline suggests. Third, would you have spent that money anyway? Only spending you would have done regardless counts as real savings; anything you buy just to "use up" the credit is not a discount, it is extra spending. If the answers are unclear, value the credit at zero and compare the deals purely on their base price. This approach keeps a large-but-restricted credit from fooling you into overpaying, and it often reveals that a plainer deal with a lower price and no credit is the better buy once the marketing is stripped away.

Key fact: A resort credit is worth only what you can actually spend under its terms. Read the restrictions before you value it, because a $200 credit you can't fully use is not $200 off your trip.

The practical move is to ask three questions before you count a credit as value: where can it be spent, does it expire before I can use it, and would I have bought those extras anyway. If the answers are murky, value the credit at zero and compare the deals on real price. Browse live vacation deals and read our vacpack explainer to keep the base price, not the bonus, at the center of your decision.

Bottom Line Up Front: "Per couple" pricing means the deal price is for two people together, not per person, and both partners are typically required to attend the presentation. When a vacation deal is quoted "per couple," the phrase is doing more than describing the price. It is describing who the resort wants in the room and why, and it shapes who can even book the offer.

What does "per couple" pricing mean?

"Per couple" pricing means the advertised price covers two people traveling and attending together, not a single traveler and not a per-person rate you multiply. The package is designed and priced around a pair, and the pair is usually required to be a married or cohabiting couple who both show up for the sales presentation. Book solo and you often find the deal is unavailable or repriced.

Why do resorts require both partners to attend?

Because timeshare sales close best when both decision-makers are present. A common objection, "I need to talk to my spouse," evaporates when the spouse is sitting right there, so resorts build the requirement into the offer. That is why the qualification call screens marital status and why "per couple" and "both must attend" almost always travel together in the fine print. The pricing model and the sales strategy are the same thing.

What to confirm before booking a per-couple deal

If you are a married or cohabiting couple, the main thing to verify is that both partners can attend the presentation on the same day, since that is almost always required. Discovering the couple requirement on the qualification call, after you have planned around the headline price, is a common and avoidable frustration. title: The Qualification Call: What They Ask & Why
metaTitle: The Qualification Call: What They Ask & Why | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A qualification call screens vacation-deal buyers by age, income, and marital status before honoring the price. Here is what they ask, why, and how to prepare.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A qualification call is the screening conversation a resort or broker holds before honoring a cheap vacation-deal price. It confirms you fit the buyer profile, commonly age 25+, a household income around $50K+, and, for couples, both partners attending, because the discount is only offered to people who could plausibly buy a timeshare.
heroImageAlt: Qualification call explained — the screening for age, income, and marital status before booking
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A qualification call is the screening conversation that happens before a resort honors a discounted vacpack price. It verifies you match the buyer profile, commonly 25 or older, roughly $50K+ household income, and both partners attending for couples, because the cheap stay is only offered to viable sales prospects.

The bargain price you saw advertised is conditional, and the qualification call is where those conditions get checked. It feels like booking logistics, but it is really a filter that decides whether you get the deal at all.

What is a qualification call?

A qualification call is a pre-booking screening conversation in which a resort or broker confirms you meet the eligibility requirements before honoring the discounted price. They ask about your age, income, marital status, and sometimes whether you already own with the brand. If you don't fit the profile, the advertised price can be withdrawn or changed, because the discount exists to attract buyers, not just guests.

What do they ask on the qualification call and why?

They ask your age (commonly 25 or older), your household income (often around $50,000 or more), your marital or cohabitation status, and whether you can attend the presentation, sometimes with a valid credit card on file. Each question maps to the resort's buyer profile: age and income signal purchasing power, couple status ensures both decision-makers attend, and the credit card signals financial standing. The call is a sales filter dressed as a booking step, closely tied to per-couple pricing.

Why does the qualification call matter to a shopper?

Because it determines whether the price you saw is a price you can get. Roughly 47% of the deals we track openly disclose a required presentation, and the qualification call is the gate to those deals. Knowing what they will ask lets you confirm you qualify before you get attached to an offer, and lets you spot when a call drifts from screening into a premature sales pitch. It is also your chance to ask hard questions: exact presentation length, total price, and any resort fees.

How to handle the qualification call well

Answer the screening questions honestly, because misrepresenting your income or marital status to secure a price can void the deal when you arrive. But remember the call runs both ways: while they qualify you, you should qualify the deal. Before you hang up, get four things confirmed, ideally in writing or by email: the exact out-of-pocket price, the precise presentation length, whether both partners must attend, and any resort fees or deposits charged separately. If the representative dodges these or starts pitching ownership on the call itself, treat that as a preview of the pressure to come. Note that a soft credit check may occur during screening, which does not affect your score, but you should not be authorizing anything that triggers a hard inquiry at this stage. A well-handled qualification call leaves you certain of the total cost and the commitments before you ever pack a bag.

Key fact: The qualification call is a filter, not a formality. If you don't fit the buyer profile, the cheap price can vanish, because the resort is buying access to prospects, not renting rooms.

Treat the call as a two-way screening: they qualify you, and you qualify the deal. Confirm the real out-of-pocket price, the exact tour length, and whether both partners must attend, then compare against live vacation deals. Reading our vacpack and per-couple pricing explainers first means you will recognize every requirement before the representative raises it. Going in with those numbers already confirmed turns the qualification call from a gate you nervously hope to pass into a short, businesslike conversation where you hold as much information as the person on the other end.

title: Tour Waiver: Paying to Skip the Presentation
metaTitle: Tour Waiver: Paying to Skip the Presentation | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A tour waiver lets you pay a fee to skip the timeshare sales presentation while keeping the discounted stay. Here is how it works and when it's worth the money.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A tour waiver is an optional fee you pay to skip the timeshare sales presentation while keeping your discounted stay. It effectively buys back the 90-120 minutes the tour would cost you, and it's worth it when your time is worth more than the fee.
heroImageAlt: Tour waiver explained — a fee to skip the 90-120 minute presentation and keep the stay
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A tour waiver is an optional fee that lets you skip the sales presentation attached to a discounted stay while keeping the deal. It buys back the 90-120 minutes the tour would take, and it makes sense whenever that time, and avoiding the pitch, is worth more to you than the waiver fee.

Not every resort offers one, but when it exists, the tour waiver is the cleanest way to enjoy a subsidized stay without sitting through the sales pitch. It turns the presentation from an obligation into a priced option.

What is a tour waiver?

A tour waiver is an optional fee you pay to be released from the presentation requirement while still receiving the discounted stay. Instead of trading your time for the deal, you trade a modest amount of money. The resort recovers some of its subsidy from the fee, and you skip the preview presentation entirely, keeping the room, the credit, and any perks that came with it.

When is a tour waiver worth paying for?

A tour waiver is worth it when the fee costs you less than the value of the time and hassle you avoid. A typical presentation runs 90-120 minutes, and in our tracked data disclosed tours average 116 minutes, but that is the floor; engaged prospects can be kept far longer. If a waiver costs, say, less than you would pay to reclaim two-plus hours of vacation and dodge a high-pressure pitch, it is an easy yes. If it approaches the cost of just booking a no-strings stay, skip it.

Comparing tour-attendance options. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does a tour waiver matter to a shopper?

Because it puts a clear price on your time and lets you opt out of the sales environment without losing the discount. It also reveals the real structure of the deal: if the resort will sell you out of the presentation for a fee, the presentation was always the product they were really after. Knowing a waiver exists lets you ask for it up front rather than assuming the tour is mandatory.

How to decide on a tour waiver

Do the math explicitly. Estimate what two-plus hours of your vacation are worth to you and add the value of avoiding a high-pressure sales pitch, then compare that against the waiver fee. If the waiver costs clearly less, buy it and reclaim your time. If it approaches the price of simply booking a stay with no presentation attached, skip the waiver and book a clean, obligation-free trip instead. Always ask whether a waiver exists before assuming the tour is mandatory, because the answer itself is revealing: a resort that will sell you out of the presentation confirms the presentation, not the room, was the real product. Also confirm the waiver preserves your discounted rate and any included perks, so you are not trading away the value that made the deal attractive. Framed as a simple time-versus-money trade, the tour waiver is one of the few points in this process where you hold the leverage.

Key fact: A tour waiver is optional and not always offered. Always ask whether one is available and exactly what it costs, because the answer reveals how much the resort values your attendance versus your money.

If no waiver is offered and you dread the pitch, remember you can also just book a stay with no presentation at all. Our tracked inventory shows a $199 median short-stay price and 168 deals under $100 with no tour attached. Compare live vacation deals and read our qualification call explainer to weigh a waiver against simply paying for a clean, obligation-free trip.

title: Bonus Week: The Add-On Vacation Explained
metaTitle: Bonus Week: The Add-On Vacation Explained | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A bonus week is an extra discounted stay a timeshare or exchange company offers on top of your normal usage. Here is what it costs, its limits, and the catches.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A bonus week is an extra, deeply discounted stay a timeshare developer or exchange company offers on top of your regular usage. It sounds like a free vacation, but bonus weeks come with a rental fee, restricted resorts and dates, and short booking windows that limit their real value.
heroImageAlt: Bonus week explained — an extra discounted stay with a fee, date limits, and short windows
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: A bonus week is an additional discounted stay offered on top of your normal timeshare usage, often by the developer or an exchange company. It is not truly free: you pay a rental-style fee, and availability is limited to certain resorts, off-peak dates, and short booking windows.

Bonus weeks get pitched as a generous extra, and sometimes they are a genuine value. But the word "bonus" hides a fee and a set of restrictions that decide whether the offer is actually useful to you.

What is a bonus week?

A bonus week is an extra discounted stay made available beyond your regular timeshare entitlement, typically by your developer or exchange company, in exchange for a reduced rental fee. It is inventory the network wants to fill, so it is offered cheaply to owners as a perk. You are effectively renting unsold time at a discount, not receiving a second week of ownership.

What are the catches with a bonus week?

The catches are fees, dates, and windows. Bonus weeks carry a rental fee, so "bonus" means cheaper, not free. They are usually limited to specific resorts with open inventory, restricted to off-peak or shoulder dates, and bookable only within short windows close to the travel date. Some also expire if unused and can't be combined with other benefits. These limits mirror the availability squeeze on float weeks: the offer is real, but only if the calendar cooperates.

DatesUsually off-peak or shoulder only

Typical bonus-week restrictions. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does a bonus week matter to a shopper?

Because it is worth comparing against the open market, not accepting as automatically free money. A bonus week's fee plus its restrictions might still beat a normal booking for the right dates, or it might cost about the same as simply booking a discounted stay yourself. Our tracked inventory shows a $199 median short-stay price and an average around $94 per night, so if a bonus week's all-in cost lands near those numbers without the date restrictions, the open market may serve you better.

How to judge whether a bonus week is a deal

Total the real cost first: the bonus-week rental fee plus any resort charges, taxes, or add-ons that stack on top. Then check the restrictions against your actual plans, do the allowed resorts and dates match a trip you genuinely want, or are you being nudged toward off-season inventory you would not otherwise choose? A cheap week you cannot use when you need it is not a bargain. Compare that all-in cost against booking the same nights on the open market, where our tracked short stays run a $199 median. If the bonus week wins on price and fits your calendar, take it; if it merely fills the resort's empty rooms at a time that suits them, pass. Also confirm the expiration and booking-window rules, since many bonus weeks must be used within a tight period or are forfeited. Judged on total cost and fit rather than the word "bonus," these offers are sometimes worthwhile and often not.

Key fact: A bonus week is discounted inventory the network wants filled, not a gift. Always compare the total fee, including any resort charges, against booking the same nights on the open market before assuming it's a deal.

The practical test is simple: total the bonus-week fee and any add-on charges, check whether the allowed dates and resorts actually match your plans, then compare against live vacation deals. If the bonus week wins on price and fits your calendar, take it. Read our exchange company explainer too, since bonus weeks and exchanges often flow through the same systems and share the same availability limits. In the end, the word "bonus" is doing marketing work, so ignore it and treat the offer like any other booking: a total price, a set of dates, and a simple question of whether it beats what you could get elsewhere for the trip you actually want.

title: RCI & Interval International: Exchange Companies 101
metaTitle: RCI & Interval International: Exchange Companies 101 | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: An exchange company like RCI or Interval International lets timeshare owners trade a week for stays at other resorts. Here is how exchanges and fees work.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: An exchange company, such as RCI or Interval International, is a network that lets timeshare owners deposit their week or points and trade for stays at thousands of other resorts. It adds flexibility, but you pay membership dues plus per-exchange fees, and desirable trades depend on what you deposit and when.
heroImageAlt: Exchange company explained — RCI and Interval let owners trade weeks, for dues and fees
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: An exchange company like RCI or Interval International lets timeshare owners deposit their week or points and swap for stays at other resorts worldwide. It solves the "stuck at one resort" problem, but you pay annual membership dues and a fee per exchange, and the trade you can get depends on the demand of what you deposit.

A timeshare tied to a single resort would get boring fast, so the industry built exchange networks. They are the reason owners can trade a week in one place for a stay somewhere else, and they are also a recurring cost layered on top of ownership.

What is an exchange company?

An exchange company is a third-party network, most prominently RCI and Interval International, that lets timeshare owners deposit their usage, a week or points, into a pool and book stays at other member resorts in return. It functions like a global trading system for timeshare time, expanding a single-resort ownership into access to thousands of properties. Your home resort is usually affiliated with one of these networks, which determines the pool you can trade within.

How do exchange fees and trading power work?

You pay to play at two levels: annual membership dues to belong to the exchange, and a separate exchange fee each time you complete a trade. On top of that, what you can pull out depends on your "trading power", the demand for the week or points you deposit. Deposit a high-demand peak week and you can pull strong trades; deposit a low-demand off-season week and your options shrink. This mirrors the availability pressure seen with float weeks and points systems.

General exchange-company cost structure. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does an exchange company matter to a shopper?

Because it is another recurring cost salespeople fold into the "lifetime of vacations" pitch without spelling out. Exchange dues and per-trade fees stack on top of your annual maintenance fee, and the flexibility is only as good as your trading power and the network's availability. When you tally the true cost of ownership, membership plus exchange fees plus maintenance, the per-night figure can rise well above the roughly $94 average per night in our tracked inventory.

How to weigh exchange access before buying

Ask which network your prospective home resort belongs to, RCI or Interval International, and what the annual membership dues and per-exchange fees currently run, because both stack on top of your maintenance fee. Then be honest about how often you would actually deposit your week and trade, since the flexibility only pays off if you use it. Understand trading power: if your home week is low-demand off-season, the trades you can pull may disappoint, so the network's brochure of thousands of resorts overstates what is realistically available to you. Add every recurring cost, membership, exchange fees, and maintenance, then divide by the nights you would genuinely book to get a true per-night figure, and compare it against booking discounted stays directly. Exchange networks reward active, flexible owners who deposit desirable weeks, and they quietly drain value from everyone else through fees, so the honest usage question decides whether the access is worth paying for.

Key fact: An exchange membership is a separate, ongoing cost. Dues and per-exchange fees are layered on top of maintenance fees, so factor all three in when judging whether ownership beats booking stays a la carte.

Exchange networks genuinely add value for owners who use them actively and deposit desirable weeks. For everyone else, the fees can erode the benefit. Before assuming exchange access justifies ownership, total every recurring cost and compare it against booking live vacation deals directly. Read our maintenance fee explainer to see how these costs compound year after year.

title: ROFR in Timeshares: Why Resale Buyers Care
metaTitle: ROFR in Timeshares: Why Resale Buyers Care | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Right of first refusal lets a timeshare developer match and take a resale before you buy it. Here is how ROFR works and why resale buyers must plan for it.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Right of first refusal (ROFR) is a contract clause that lets the timeshare developer step in and buy a resale at the agreed price before your purchase closes. It means a developer can "take" a resale deal you negotiated, which shapes how resale buyers price offers and how long deals take to close.
heroImageAlt: ROFR explained — a developer's right to match and take a timeshare resale before you close
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: Right of first refusal (ROFR) is a clause that lets the timeshare developer match the price on a resale and buy the interest itself before your purchase closes. In practice it means a developer can intercept a resale deal you negotiated, which is why resale buyers watch it closely and why some cheap resale offers never close.

The timeshare resale market is where prices are often near zero, but a clause called right of first refusal can quietly stand between a resale buyer and the deal they thought they had. Understanding it explains a lot of resale-market behavior.

What is right of first refusal in timeshares?

Right of first refusal is a contract provision giving the developer the right to step into a resale transaction, match the agreed price, and buy the interest itself instead of letting the outside buyer complete the purchase. When a resale is under contract, it is submitted to the developer, who can either waive ROFR and let the sale proceed or exercise it and take the deal at the buyer's price. Either way, the developer decides.

Why do resale buyers care about ROFR?

Because it can kill a deal or delay it, and it sets a floor on how low a resale price can realistically go. If a buyer negotiates a rock-bottom price, the developer may exercise ROFR to reacquire the interest cheaply, and the buyer walks away empty-handed after weeks of waiting. So resale buyers price offers with ROFR in mind, sometimes bidding a little higher to clear the developer's likely threshold, and build in time for the review. It is a major reason a resale can take longer than a normal purchase to close.

StepWhat happens
Resale under contractBuyer and seller agree a price
Submitted to developerDeveloper reviews under ROFR
Developer waivesSale proceeds to the outside buyer
Developer exercisesDeveloper buys it; outside buyer is out

How a ROFR review typically unfolds. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Why does ROFR matter to a shopper?

Because it explains the friction in the resale market and reinforces how little most timeshares are worth on resale. A clause that lets the developer scoop up bargain resales tells you the developer values controlling its own inventory more than the interest is worth to outside buyers. For most travelers chasing a cheap trip, ROFR is one more reason the resale rabbit hole isn't worth it, when you can simply book a discounted stay with no ownership at all.

How to navigate ROFR if you're set on a resale

First, find out whether your target resort even uses ROFR, since not all do. Where it applies, price your offer knowing the developer can match it: bidding at rock-bottom invites the developer to exercise its right and take the deal, leaving you with nothing after weeks of waiting. Many resale buyers research recent ROFR outcomes for a given resort to gauge the price threshold the developer tends to let pass, then bid just above it. Build the review period into your timeline, because a resale is never final until the developer waives, and that adds delay a normal purchase does not have. Keep your deposit terms contingent on the developer waiving ROFR so you are protected if it exercises. And weigh all of this against the reality that most timeshares resell for near nothing precisely because the obligation never ends, which for many travelers makes booking a discounted stay far simpler than chasing a resale.

Key fact: ROFR gives the developer, not the seller, the final say on a resale. Even a signed resale contract can be intercepted, so a resale is never truly done until the developer waives its right of first refusal.

If you are set on a resale, budget time for the ROFR review and price your offer knowing the developer can match it. But if your real goal is a cheap vacation rather than ownership, skip the complexity entirely: our tracked inventory shows short vacpacks with a $199 median and 168 deals under $100. Compare live vacation deals and read our deeded vs right-to-use explainer before wading into the resale market.

title: The "Viking Ship" Myth: Perpetuity Clauses Explained
metaTitle: The Viking Ship Myth: Perpetuity Clauses Explained | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: The "Viking ship clause" is a timeshare forum legend about perpetuity contracts binding heirs. Here is what is true about perpetual clauses and what is not.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: The "Viking ship clause" is a piece of timeshare forum folklore: the colorful claim that a perpetuity contract binds you and your descendants forever, the way a Viking would be chained to his ship. The legend is an exaggeration, but it points at a real feature, perpetual "in perpetuity" clauses that can outlive the original owner.
heroImageAlt: Viking ship clause myth — forum legend about perpetuity contracts, and the real feature behind it
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: The "Viking ship clause" is timeshare forum folklore, a memorable nickname for perpetuity contracts that supposedly chain owners and their heirs to a timeshare forever. The vivid "bound to the ship" story is an exaggeration, but it dramatizes something real: many timeshare contracts run "in perpetuity," meaning the obligation, including maintenance fees, can continue indefinitely and pass to an estate.

If you have read timeshare forums, you have probably seen someone warn about the "Viking ship clause." It is not a legal term of art; it is community shorthand born from frustration. Separating the myth from the real contract feature is worth doing, because the underlying concept genuinely matters.

What is the "Viking ship clause"?

The "Viking ship clause" is a forum nickname, not an actual named clause, for perpetuity provisions in timeshare contracts that owners feel bind them, and even their descendants, for life and beyond. The imagery, an oarsman chained to a Viking longship, captures the feeling of being unable to escape. No contract literally uses the phrase, and the legend overstates the mechanics, but it stuck because it names a real anxiety: getting out of a perpetual timeshare can be genuinely hard.

What's actually true about perpetuity clauses?

What's true is that many deeded timeshares are sold "in perpetuity," meaning the interest does not automatically expire. Because it is real property that can be inherited, the obligation, principally the annual maintenance fee, can continue indefinitely and pass to an owner's estate or heirs unless the interest is sold, transferred, or otherwise disposed of. What's not true is the fatalistic part of the legend: heirs are generally not forced to accept an inherited timeshare, an estate can decline or disclaim it, and owners can pursue transfer, deed-back, or resale, though none of these are guaranteed or easy. The clause makes exit difficult, not impossible.

A FAM trip is a familiarization trip: a subsidized or free resort stay offered to acquaint someone with the property in the hope they book it, sell it, or refer it in the future. metaDescription: Drip pricing reveals mandatory fees gradually during checkout so the first price looks lower. Here is how it works in travel and how to see the real total.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Drip pricing is a tactic where a business advertises a low headline price, then reveals mandatory fees one at a time as you move through checkout, so the final total is higher than it first appeared. In travel it shows up as resort fees, booking fees, and service charges added late, and it's a focus of FTC scrutiny.

content:
Bottom Line Up Front: Drip pricing is a tactic where a low headline price is advertised, then mandatory fees are revealed gradually during checkout so the real total ends up higher than it first looked. In travel this appears as resort fees, booking fees, and service charges added late in the process. It's a pattern regulators, including the FTC, actively scrutinize.

Drip pricing is why the price you clicked is almost never the price you pay. It works by controlling the order in which you see costs, hooking you with a low number and revealing the rest once you're committed. Naming the tactic is the first step to defeating it.

What is drip pricing?

Drip pricing is a pricing practice in which mandatory charges are disclosed incrementally, one "drip" at a time, during the purchase process, rather than shown together in the first advertised price. The initial number is real but incomplete, and by the time all the compulsory fees have appeared, the total is meaningfully higher. Because the fees are mandatory, not optional add-ons, the low headline price was never actually available.

How does drip pricing show up in travel deals?

In travel it typically arrives as resort fees, cleaning or service fees, booking fees, and taxes that surface only at later checkout steps. You start with an attractive nightly rate, proceed through several screens, and watch mandatory charges accumulate before the final total. This is a cousin of the rack rate illusion: both manipulate the numbers you see to shape your perception, one by inflating the "before" price and the other by hiding parts of the "after" price. Regulators treat undisclosed mandatory fees as a consumer-protection concern.

When you consistently compare final totals rather than headline rates, the tactic loses its edge, and the cheapest-looking deal often turns out to be the most expensive once its drips are added up.
